transcript.content: Hello, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Yeah, I came in because I just feel really restless all the time when I’m supposed to sit still. Like in the radiology suite or in class, it feels like I’m crawling out of my skin. I’ve tried to just tough it out for months, but I still end up pacing, shifting around, or finding some excuse to get up and move.
Have you started or changed any new medications recently, such as antipsychotics, anti-nausea drugs, or other prescriptions, before this restlessness began?
I don’t think so. I’m not on anything new that I can think of, and I haven’t changed any prescriptions recently.
When you feel this need to move or pace, do you also notice worried thoughts or a sense of anxiety alongside it, or is it mainly just a physical urge to move without any accompanying worry?

It’s mainly a physical urge, I think. Like when I’m in the radiology suite or sitting in class, I just feel like I’m crawling out of my skin and I have to move. I’ll start shifting around, pacing if I can, or finding some reason to get up. It’s not really that I’m sitting there worrying about something specific.
Did you notice this kind of restlessness and need to move back when you were a child or teenager, or is this something that started only recently as an adult?

No, it’s definitely not just recent. My parents still bring up stuff from elementary school conferences—teachers saying I was always getting out of my seat, calling out, or rushing ahead before they’d even finished giving directions. So it was happening way before middle school, not just since I started radiology training.

Does this restlessness and impulsivity cause problems for you in more than one area of your life right now—for example, both at work and at home or in social situations—or is it mostly limited to one setting?

It’s definitely not just one setting. The biggest problems are in my clinical rotations—my evaluations have dropped, and I got put on a formal remediation plan because supervisors say I’m disrupting patient flow and making teamwork harder. I’m honestly worried that if I can’t get it under control, it could cost me my spot in the program.
Aside from the restlessness and impulsivity, do you also struggle with staying focused on tasks, losing track of details, or forgetting things you need to do, both in training and in daily life?

I’m not really sure. I mean, I can get distracted like anyone, but the thing that stands out to me is more the needing to move and acting before I think. I haven’t really noticed a big pattern of forgetting things or losing details, at least not compared to the restlessness.
Do you often find yourself interrupting conversations, blurting out answers before someone finishes a question, or having trouble waiting your turn in lines or discussions?

Yeah, I do that a lot. Like when a supervisor is explaining a positioning step or asking me something, I’ll jump in with the answer before they’re even done. Then a second later I realize I missed the part they were actually trying to tell me, and it makes me look like I wasn’t listening.

Have you ever had distinct periods—lasting several days or more—where you felt unusually elated, needed much less sleep than normal, or felt like your thoughts were racing much more than usual, separate from how you feel most of the time?

I don’t think so. I haven’t noticed anything like a stretch of days where I’m unusually euphoric or barely sleeping and still feeling great. My energy can feel high, but it doesn’t really come in those separate episodes like that.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports chronic, pervasive motor restlessness (pacing, difficulty sitting still), impulsivity (blurting out answers, interrupting before others finish), and hyperactivity that began in childhood (documented by teacher reports in elementary school) and persists into adulthood. Symptoms occur across multiple settings (clinical rotations, classroom) and cause functional impairment (remediation plan, risk to training program). Inattentive symptoms (forgetfulness, losing track of details) are minimal/denied, supporting a predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation rather than combined type. Medication-induced akathisia was ruled out (no new drug exposure), and the restlessness lacks the cognitive worry typical of anxiety disorders, making generalized anxiety disorder less likely. Bipolar/hypomanic episodes were explicitly denied (no distinct periods of elevated mood, decreased sleep, or racing thoughts), excluding mood disorder as the cause of hyperactivity.
